Mr. Averill, on leave, introduced the following bill: A Bill Confirming articles of agreement with Shoshone and Bannock tribe of Indians, and directing the Secretary of the Interior to carry the same into effect. Whereas by act of Congress approved June firth, eighteen hundred and seventy-two, entitled An act to authorize the President of the United States to negotiate with the chiefs and head-men of the Shoshone and Bannock tribe of Indians for the relinquishment of a portion of their reservation in Wyoming Territory power is given the President to make such negotiation; and Whereas said act makes it the duty of the President to report his proceedings thereunder to Congress for approval or rejections; and Whereas the President did, through his duly-authorized commissioner, negotiate and make with said Indians the following agreement, to wit: Whereas it appears by the records of the above negotiation, now on file in the office of the Commissioner of Indian Affairs, that the provisions of said act of Congress directing the exchange of lands, acre for acre, with said Indians, was not desired by them, but the above and foregoing agreement for the cession to the United States of a portion of their reservation, according to the provisions therein contained, being preferred by them, is accepted by the United States: Therefore,

title: A Bill Confirming articles of agreement with Shoshone and Bannock tribe of Indians, and directing the Secretary of the Interior to carry the same into effect.

Neugardt issued and delivered to the said Jacob Neugardt; and Whereas the said Jacob Neugardt afterward repudiated the transaction, denied the deposit of the money for the purpose aforesaid, and brought suit and recovered judgment against the said James W. Bowen in the courts of Pennsylvania, and he, the said James W. Bowen, was compelled to refund the sum out of his own private means: Therefore,

title: A Bill For the relief of James W. Bowen, late provost-marshal of the tenth congressional district of Pennsylvania.

Mr. Packard, on leave, introduced the following bill: A Bill To authorize the President of the United States to request the republic of Hayti to indemnify Antonio Pelletier. Whereas Antonio Pelletier, a citizen of the United States, naturalized in the year eighteen hundred and fifty-two, did, during the month of August or September, eighteen hundred and sixty, purchase of a United States marshal, at public auction, at the port of Key West, the bark William; and the subsequently the said Pelletier shipped a crew and placed a cargo of merchandise on board the said vessel and proceeded on a trading voyage to the West Indies; and that while in pursuance of his said legitimate commercial enterprise his said vessel, under stress of weather, was cast upon a reef, designated as Caico, off the coast of Hayti, in the mouth of February, eighteen hundred and sixty-one, and after drifting for several days the bark came to anchor in the port of Fort Liberte, Hayti; and that after making some slight repairs, and being informed that the port of Fort Liberte was not open to commerce, anchor was weighed and the bark proceeded down the bay until near the fort, when the prevailing breeze failed, and the vessel drifted on the reef opposite the fort, where the tide left her high and dry, when certain authorities of the republic of Hayti boarded the said bark William, arrested the said Antonio Pelletier and his crew, and carried them ashore and consigned them to prison, without cause or proper trial, holding the said Pelletier, the master and owner of the vessel aforesaid, a close prisoner for the period of nearly three years, condemning him to death, and subjecting him to the most cruel treatment, from which he finally escaped by the assistance of the agents of foreign governments; and that during his imprisonment his said vessel and cargo were seized and confiscated by the authorities of the republic of Hayti; and that his said imprisonment, spoliation, and consequent losses amounted to the financial damages of the said Pelletier in the sum of six hundred and thirteen thousand eight hundred dollars; and further, that the imprisonment and inhuman treatment to which the said Pelletier was subjected resulted in the serious impairing of his health, and rendered him an invalid and crippled for life, for which afflictions it is almost impossible to estimate in moneyed damages; and Whereas the facts above recited are evidenced by executive document numbered two hundred and sixty, second session of the Fortieth Congress, furnished by the Secretary of State in response to House resolution of the tenth March, anno Domini eighteen hundred and sixty-eight: Now, therefore,

title: A Bill To authorize the President of the United States to request the republic of Hayti to indemnify Antonio Pelletier.

latestAction.text: Read twice, referred to the Committee on Commerce, and ordered to be printed. Mr. Stevenson, on leave, introduced the following bill: A Bill To accept the Louisville and Portland Canal, and to reduce the tolls thereof. Whereas the stock of the Louisville and Portland Canal Company is owned and held by the United States, expecting five shares held by the directors of said company; and Whereas said canal has been enlarged chiefly by the United States; and Whereas it is practically part of the Ohio River and necessary to the navigation of that stream; and Whereas the tolls now charged and collected by said company are excessive and burdensome to commerce; and Whereas the State of Kentucky has, by her legislature, adopted the following resolution for the transfer of said canal, and the property of said company connected therewith, to the United States, to wit: Resolution in relation to the Louisville and Portland Canal. "Whereas All the stock in the Louisville and Portland Canal belongs to the United States Government except five shares owned by the directors of the Louisville and Portland Canal Company; and said directors under the authority of the legislation of Kentucky and the United States executed a mortgage to secure bonds named in said mortgage some of which are out and unpaid; and said canal company may owe other debts; and "Whereas it is right and proper that the Government of the United States should assume the control and management of said canal: Therefore "Be it resolved by the general assembly of the commonwealth of Kentucky That the president and directors of the Louisville and Portland Canal Company are hereby authorized and directed to surrender the said canal all the property connected therewith to the Government of the United States upon the following terms and conditions: "First that the Government of the United States shall not levy tolls upon said canal except so much as may be necessary to keep the same in repair pay all necessary superintendence custody and expense and make all necessary improvements. "Secondly that the city of Louisville shall have the right to throw bridges over the canal at such points as said city may deem proper: Provided always That said bridges shall be so located as not to interfere with the use of the canal and so constructed as not to interfere with its navigation. "Thirdly that the title and possession of the United States of said canal shall not interfere with the right of the State to serve criminal and civil processes and with the State's general police powers over the territory covered by the said canal and appendages. "Fourthly and further that the city of Louisville shall at all times have the right of drainage into said canal: Provided That the connections between the drains and canal shall be made upon the most approved plan to keep out mud and garbage. "Fifthly that the use of the water-power of said canal shall be guaranteed forever to the actual owners of property contiguous to said canal its branches and dams subject to such restrictions and regulations as may be made by the Secretary of that Department of the United States Government which may have charge of the said canal. "Sixthly that the Government of the United States shall before such surrender discharge said mortgage and pay all debts due by the said canal company and purchase the stock of said directors."

title: A Bill To accept the Louisville and Portland Canal, and to reduce the tolls thereof.

Whereas the Government of the United States holds three bonds, signed by the governor of the State of Tennessee, dated the first day of June, eighteen hundred and sixty-six, one for three hundred and thirty-seven thousand nine hundred and ninety-three dollars and seventy-three cents; another for ninety-four thousand one hundred and forty-two dollars and eighty-five cents; and the other for twenty-one thousand six hundred and sixty-one dollars and seventy-three cents, all bearing interest at the rate of seven and three-tenths per centum per annum, and payable to the United States of America, for property and railway material purchased by the Edgefield and Kentucky, and the Memphis, Clarksville and Louisville Railroads, and all of them entitled to credits for certain mail-service which is not in dispute; and Whereas the State of Tennessee claims an abatement in the amount of said bonds, and alleges as a reason therefor that the property was purchased by receivers in charge of said roads for the use and benefit of the companies then owning them, and at extravagant prices, and said State, after the property was placed in the possession of the companies, executed the bonds aforesaid, to prevent the stopping of said roads, by a seizure and removal of the rolling-stock from said roads by the officers and agents of the United States Government, and that, inasmuch as said companies are utterly insolvent, and unable to pay any part of said bonds, that the State should only be charged with the actual value of the property at the date of the sale; and said State also claims credit by the value of bridges and other property of said roads destroyed while run by the United States Government; and Whereas the said State of Tennessee claims other credits by railroad iron, spikes, cars, ties, and other property taken from the Winchester and Alabama Railroad in eighteen hundred and sixty-three, used and appropriated by the United States Government: Therefore,

title: A Bill For the relief of the State of Tennessee.

latestAction.text: Read twice, referred to the Committee on the Judiciary, and ordered to be printed. Mr. Shanks, on leave, introduced the following bill: A Bill Establishing a United States district court in the Indian country. Whereas the several treaties between the United States and the Cherokee, Choctaw, Chickasaw, Creek, and Seminole Nations of Indians, concluded in eighteen hundred and sixty-six, provide for the establishment of a United States court in the Indian country, commonly known as the Indian Territory, as follows, viz: The Cherokee treaty, article thirteenth: The Cherokees also agree that a court or courts may be established by the United States in said Territory with such jurisdiction and organized in such manner as may be prescribed by law: Provided That the judicial tribunals of the nation shall be allowed to retain exclusive jurisdiction in all civil and criminal causes arising within their country in which members of the nation by nativity or adoption shall be the only parties or where the cause of action shall arise in the Cherokee Nation except as otherwise provided in the treaty." The Choctaw and Chickasaw treaty article eighth section eighth: "The Choctaws and Chickasaws also agree that a court or courts may be established in said Territory with such jurisdiction and organization as Congress may prescribe: Provided That the same shall not interfere with the local judiciary of either of said nations." The Greek treaty article tenth: "The Creeks agree to such legislation as Congress and the President of the United States may deem necessary for the better administration of justice and the protection of the rights of persons and property within the Indian Territory: Provided however That said legislation shall not in any manner interfere with or annul their present tribal organization rights laws privileges and customs." "The Creeks also agree that a court or courts may be established in said Territory with such jurisdiction and organized in such manner as Congress may by law provide." The Seminole treaty article seventh "The Seminole Nation agree to such legislation as Congress and the President deem necessary for the better administration of the rights of the person and property within the Indian Territory: Provided however That said legislation shall not in any manner interfere with or annul their present tribal organization rights laws privileges and customs." "The Seminoles also agree that a court or courts may be established in said Territory with such jurisdiction and organized in such manner as Congress may by law provide:" Therefore

title: A Bill Establishing a United States district court in the Indian country.

latestAction.text: Read twice, referred to the Committee of Claims, and ordered to be printed. Mr. Sheldon, on leave, introduced the following bill: A Bill For the relief of Henry Ware. Whereas agents of the Government of the United States seized seven hundred and fifty-eight bales of cotton, at Shreveport, in the State of Louisiana, on the first day of December, eighteen hundred and sixty-five, the property of Henry Ware, then of Harrison County, Texas, now of Louisiana, on the false pretext that fifty-five bales thereof had been the property of the late confederate government, and under certain proceedings instituted in the State court for the recovery of said cotton by the owner thereof, the sheriff took possession of the same, and was immediately thereafter forcibly dispossessed by United States troops, by order of the commander of the post of Shreveport, and said agents sent said cotton to New Orleans, where it was held by the United States until the sixth day of March, eighteen hundred and sixty-six; and Whereas while said cotton was so held by the United States at New Orleans, the owner thereof twice petitioned the department commander, Major General E. R. S. Canby, for permission to institute an action in the United States district court for the recovery thereof, and was refused, and was assured by said department commander that the possession of said cotton would be forcibly maintained; and Whereas when the United States restored said cotton to its lawful owner, said Henry Ware, it was deficient in quantity and inferior in quality, and was worth fifty-three thousand nine hundred and seventy-one dollars and sixty-one cents less than when so seized, and the United States compelled said Ware to pay excessive and unlawful charges on said cotton, amounting to ten thousand eight hundred and forty-two dollars and thirty-one cents, as the condition of the restoration thereof; and Whereas the owner of said cotton having, on the seventh day of April, eighteen hundred and sixty-six, instituted an action for the recovery of the difference in the value of the same at the time of the seizure, and the time of the restoration thereof, and also of said excessive charges, against the agents of the United States, in a State court of Louisiana, the said department commander, on the twenty-fourth day of April, eighteen hundred and sixty-six, issued his order prohibiting said court from entertaining jurisdiction of said action, but afterward, on the fourteenth day of May, eighteen hundred and sixty-six, authorized said court to entertain such jurisdiction, and the Secretary of the Treasury of the United States employed attorneys and counsel who defended said action, and judgment therein was rendered for said Ware for the difference in the value of said cotton when seized and when restored, and for the charges so paid, amounting in the aggregate to sixty-four thousand eight hundred and thirteen dollars and ninety-two cents, with interest and costs, and no part of said judgment has ever been paid: Therefore,

title: A Bill For the relief of Henry Ware.

Whereas Edward H. Wilson did, on the tenth day of July, eighteen hundred and sixty-five, institute suit against the Bank of Louisiana, in the circuit court of the State of Alabama, at Montgomery, by attachment, which was levied upon three hundred and forty-six bales of cotton, in two separate lots, one of one hundred and eighty-two bales and the other of one hundred and fifty-four bales; and afterward, by order of said circuit court, Josiah Morris replevined said cotton; and both lots of said cotton were subsequently seized and, by order of the United States district court for the middle district of Alabama, confiscated; and after such seizure, and before said order of confiscation, said Morris replevined said lot of one hundred and fifty-four bales; and subsequently John Hardy, marshal of said district court, sold said one hundred and eighty-two bales of cotton, pursuant to said order, for the sum of seventeen thousand three hundred and eighty-one dollars and five cents, and paid the same over to the clerk of said court, and the said district court rendered judgment against said Josiah Morris, on his replevin bond, for the sum of twenty-five thousand and sixty-nine dollars and seventy cents, the value of said one hundred and fifty-four bales replevined as aforesaid, which amount was paid by said Josiah Morris to said marshal John Hardy; and Whereas said marshal and clerk deposited said moneys in the First National Bank of Selma, a bank which had been duly designated by the Secretary of the Treasury as a depository of public moneys for the State of Alabama, in obedience to orders of the Secretary of the Treasury; and Whereas, upon an appeal by said Josiah Morris to the Supreme Court of the United States, said orders of said district court were reversed, and said cases were remanded and afterward dismissed in the said district court; and Whereas the said Edward H. Wilson recovered final judgment in said suit against the Bank of Louisiana, on the twelfth day of July, eighteen hundred and sixty-seven, for the sum of one hundred and six thousand nine hundred and sixty-nine dollars, by virtue of which judgment said Wilson is lawfully entitled to the money so realized on said cotton, amounting in the aggregate to the sum of forty-two thousand four hundred and fifty dollars and seventy-five cents; and Whereas no part of said moneys so deposited by said clerk and marshal was ever withdrawn from said bank; and Whereas after said deposits said bank became insolvent, and a decree of the dissolution thereof was entered in the district court of the United States for the middle district of Alabama; and Whereas the assets of said bank came into the hands of Cornelius Cadle, junior, by virtue of an appointment to receive the same, issued by the Comptroller of the Currency of the United States, and from time to time the said Cadle has paid over to the Treasurer of the United States the moneys received by him: Therefore,

title: A Bill For the relief of Edward H. Wilson.

Brooks, on leave, introduced the following bill: A Bill For the relief of the freedmen of the Choctaw and Chickasaw Nations. Whereas in the third article of the treaty made and concluded on the twenty-eighth day of April, eighteen hundred and sixty-six, between the United Slates and the Choctaw and Chickasaw Nations of Indians, it is provided that the sum of three hundred thousand dollars (the consideration for the cession of certain territory by said nations to the United States) shall be invested and held by the United States, at an interest of not less than five per centum, in trust, for the said Choctaw and Chickasaw Nations, to be paid to the same in the proportion of three-fourths to the former and one-fourth to the latter, immediately upon the enactment of such laws, rules, and regulations by their respective legislatures as may be necessary to give all persons of African descent, resident in said nations at the date of the treaty of Fort Smith, and their descendants, previously held in slavery among said nations, all the rights, privileges, and immunities, including the right of suffrage, of citizens of said nations; and on failure to pass such laws, rules, and regulations by the legislatures of said nations respectively, within two years from the ratification of said treaty, the said sum of three hundred thousand dollars shall cease to be held in trust for the said Choctaw and Chickasaw Nations, and shall be held for the use and benefit of such of said persons of African descent as the United States shall remove from said territory, in such manner as the United States shall deem proper, the United States agreeing, within ninety days from the expiration of said treaty, to remove from said nation all such persons of African descent as may be willing to remove; and Whereas, further, the said Choctaw and Chickasaw legislatures have heretofore refused, and still refuse, to pass such laws, rules, and regulations as aforesaid, but have respectively passed enactments declaring it to be the unanimous consent of said legislatures that the United States shall hold said three hundred thousand dollars for the benefit of said freedmen, and directing notice to be given to the United States that it is their wish that said persons of African descent be removed by the United States beyond the limits of said Choctaw and Chickasaw Nations respectively, according to the provisions of article three of the treaty aforesaid; and it being the desire of said freedmen to remove beyond the limits of said nations, and to receive the said sum of three hundred thousand dollars: Therefore,

title: A Bill For the relief of the freedmen of the Choctaw and Chickasaw Nations.

latestAction.text: Read twice, referred to the Committee on Private Land-Claims, and ordered to be printed. Mr. Packard, on leave, introduced the following bill: A Bill To release the title of the United States to certain lands in Michigan City, Indiana. Whereas Isaac C. Elston, on the twenty-fifth day of June, eighteen hundred and thirty-five, agreed to donate to the United States a piece or parcel of ground in Michigan City, in the State of Indiana, for a light-house, said piece or parcel of land to be two hundred and sixty feet long and one hundred and seventy-five feet wide, the courses of the lines to run parallel to the streets in said city. That on that day the said Elston, intending to convey the land so donated, executed a deed to the United States for a piece or parcel of ground, and by mistake described it as follows: All that tract or parcel of land situate lying and being in the county of Laporte in the State of Indiana and in and part of section twenty-nine in township thirty-eight north range four west bounded as follows namely: beginning at a point twenty feet west of a stake stuck for the site of a light-house and from thence south one hundred and thirty feet to a stake and from thence east one hundred and seventy-five feet to a stake and from thence north to Lake Michigan two hundred and sixty feet; thence west with the margin of the lake one hundred and seventy-five feet and from thence south to the place of beginning." That the United States soon after the execution of said deed took possession of the ground first above described and so intended to be conveyed and built a light-house thereon inclosed it with a fence and thence hitherto have held the exclusive possession thereof and have never asserted title to any other property under said deed; and Whereas the said Elston was the owner of all the land adjoining said ground and retained possession thereof and afterward sold and conveyed the same to innocent purchasers who or those claiming under such conveyances caused the same to be platted and laid out into town-lots as an addition to Michigan City and which said town-lots were laid out with reference to the land so taken possession of and fenced by the United States and which said land and town-lots are now held and possessed in good faith by the remote vendees of said Elston: Now therefore For the purpose of correcting said mistake and releasing all right title or interest which the United States may have by virtue of the error in said deed of said Elston: Therefore

title: A Bill To release the title of the United States to certain lands in Michigan City, Indiana.

Whereas Josiah Morris did, on the twenty-fifth day of March, eighteen hundred and sixty-seven, pay to John Hardy, the marshal of the United States for the middle district of Alabama, the sum of thirty-one thousand six hundred and eighty-nine dollars and fifty-five cents, on a certain execution held by said John Hardy in an action entitled as follows, to wit: The United States versus One hundred and twenty Bales of Cotton, Josiah Morris, and J. F. Johnson; in which action a judgment was rendered against said Josiah Morris and J. F. Johnson, and execution issued against the property of said Morris; And whereas the said John Hardy, marshal as aforesaid, did, on the twenty-sixth day of March, eighteen hundred and sixty-seven, deposit in the First National Bank of Selma, a bank that had been designated by the Secretary of the Treasury as a depositary of public moneys for the State of Alabama, and notice of this selection officially given to said Hardy, the sum of thirty thousand five hundred and nine dollars of the money so as aforesaid collected by him from the said Josiah Morris; And whereas said judgment was thereafter reversed by the Supreme Court of the United States, and restitution of said sum ordered, as by the judgment of said Supreme Court will appear; And it further appearing that no part of the said sum of thirty thousand five hundred and nine dollars, so deposited as aforesaid by the said Hardy, was ever withdrawn from the said First National Bank of Selma, but that the whole thereof was entered as a credit to the said Hardy upon the books of the said bank; And it further appearing that, after said deposit by the said Hardy, the said First National Bank of Selma became insolvent, and that a decree of the dissolution thereof was entered in the district court of the United States for the middle district of Alabama; And it further appearing that the assets which were of the said bank came into the hands of Cornelius Cadle, junior, esquire, by virtue of an appointment to receive the same issued by the Comptroller of the Currency of the United States; and that, from time to time, the said Cadle has paid over to the Treasurer of the United States the moneys received by him: Therefore,

title: A Bill For the relief of Josiah Morris.

Whereas in view of the rapid increase in the trade of the city of Baltimore, and the present limited character and inadequacy of the appropriations heretofore authorized by Congress to accommodate and develop said trade; and Whereas the close proximity of the city of Baltimore to the seat of tho Federal Government, as well as to the chief distributing centers of the South and West, by lines of railway already built and in operation, or proposed to be built, or in progress of construction at this time, furnishing direct communication with the nearest point upon the eastern seaboard and with foreign markets; and Whereas the port of the city of Baltimore is unsurpassed in its natural advantages, accessible at all seasons of the year, and favorable in all respects in its adaptation to the storage of merchandise intended for local consumption or export to more distant markets; and Whereas the object proposed to be accomplished by this act is strictly national in its character, looking to the direct advancement of the leading Southern and Western States, and indirectly to that large portion of the North with which Baltimore has already facilities of transit, thus holding out to all the advantages of a grand commercial and distributing center on the Atlantic seaboard, by short and direct lines of communication with the great producing centers of the West and South, and the choice of other markets, both coastwise and foreign; and Whereas both our commercial and naval marine are alike deeply interested in the liberal encouragement and building up of a grand depot for the distribution of cheap coals, or steam and manufacturing purposes, certain to result from the free and unobstructed navigation of the Patapsco River and the improvement of the harbor of Baltimore, an object of national importance as well as practical economy: Therefore

title: A Bill For the improvement of the harbor of Baltimore, in the State of Maryland, and the increase of the custom-house and revenue accommodations of said city.

Mr. McIntyre, on leave, introduced the following bill: A Bill Authorizing the Secretary of the Treasury to pay certain claims arising from the seizure and conversion, to the uses of the United States, of private personal property after the thirtieth day of June, eighteen hundred and sixty-five. Whereas the President of the United States, by proclamation bearing date May the ninth, eighteen hundred and sixty-five, declared the war at an end; and whereas, by proclamation of May the twenty-ninth, eighteen hundred and sixty-five, he directed the restoration of all private property, except as to slaves;" and whereas in obedience to the fifth section of the act of Congress approved July thirteenth eighteen hundred and sixty-one and the sixth section of Treasury Regulations approved March thirty-first eighteen hundred and sixty-three made in pursuance of said act of Congress the President by proclamation of June twenty-fourth eighteen hundred and sixty-five restored commercial intercourse between all the States of the American Union; and whereas the Secretary of the Treasury by the authority of the same issued a circular letter of instructions of date June twenty-seventh eighteen hundred and sixty-five withdrawing the authority of the Treasury Department to seize cotton of any character or description after the thirtieth day of June eighteen hundred and sixty-five; and whereas said circular letter of instructions not only forbid the seizure of all cotton after said date but simply authorized Treasury agents to receive cotton formerly the property of the Confederate States which had been theretofore surrendered to the military and naval authorities of the United States; and whereas seizures of such property were made as late as December eighteen hundred and sixty-five under the pretext that such cotton was the property of the Confederate States whereby the pretext of seizure authorized the agent to retain one-fourth of the amount seized; and whereas the owners of the property at the time of seizure had renewed their allegiance to the Government of the United States; and whereas many of said claimants for such property are barred by the statute of limitations from obtaining redress through the Court of Claims; and whereas in the United States circuit court for the district of South Carolina August term eighteen hundred and sixty-nine in the case of McLeod versus Callicott a United States Treasury agent the Chief Justice of the United States decided that all cotton seized after the thirtieth day of June eighteen hundred and sixty-five was unauthorized and therefore illegal and that the owner of such property was entitled to recover the market value thereof at the time of seizure with lawful interest from date; and whereas the Solicitor and the Attorney General of the United States have fully recognized the decision of the Chief Justice of the United States as the law in the premises; and whereas the Supreme Court of the United States in the case of the steamer Cotton Plant unanimously decided that cotton seized after the cessation of hostilities was "not captured or prize cotton therefore illegal, and directed its restoration; and whereas the twelfth section of the act of Congress approved July twenty-third, eighteen hundred and sixty-six, directs the Secretary of the Treasury to refund to the lawful owners all moneys erroneously received and erroneously covered into the Treasury: Therefore,

title: A Bill Authorizing the Secretary of the Treasury to pay certain claims arising from the seizure and conversion, to the uses of the United States, of private personal property after the thirtieth day of June, eighteen hundred and sixty-five.

Mr. Morey, on leave, introduced the following bill: A Bill For the relief of the freedmen of the Choctaw Nation, and for other purposes. Whereas in the third article of the treaty made and concluded on the twenty-eighth day of April, eighteen hundred and sixty-six, between the United States and the Choctaw and Chickasaw Nations of Indians, it is provided that the sum of three hundred thousand dollars shall be invested and held by the United States, at an interest of not less than five per centum, in trust for the said Choctaw and Chickasaw Nations, to be paid to the same in the proportion of three-fourths to the former, and one-fourth to the latter, immediately upon the enactment of such laws, rules, and regulations by their respective legislatures, as may be necessary to give all persons of African descent, resident in said nations at the date of the treaty of Fort Smith, and their descendants, previously held in slavery among said nations, all the rights, privileges, and immunities, including the right of suffrage of citizens of said nations; and on failure to pass such laws, rules, and regulations by the legislatures of said nations respectively, within two years from the ratification of said treaty, the said sum of three hundred thousand dollars shall cease to be held in trust for the said Choctaw and Chickasaw Nations, and shall be held for the use and benefit of such of said persons of African descent as the United States shall remove from said territory, the United States agreeing to remove from said nation, all such persons of African descent as may be willing to remove; and whereas, further, the said Chocktaw and Chickasaw legislatures have heretofore refused and still refuse to pass such laws, rules, and regulations as aforesaid, but have respectively passed enactments declaring it to be the unanimous consent of said legislatures that the United States shall hold said three hundred thousand dollars for the benefit of said freedmen, and directing notice to be given to the United States that it is their wish that the said persons of African descent be removed by the United States beyond the limits of said Choctaw and Chickasaw Nations respectively, according to the provisions of article third of the treaty aforesaid; and it being the desire of said freedmen to remove beyond the limits of said nations, and to receive the said sum of three hundred thousand dollars: Therefore,

title: A Bill For the relief of the freedmen of the Choctaw Nation, and for other purposes.

Mr. Palmer, on leave, introduced the following bill: A Bill To confirm the title to certain lands on the Fort Kearney military reservation in Fremont County, Iowa. Whereas the following described entries at the Council Bluffs land district, in the State of Iowa, were made on lands which had been reserved for military purposes for the use of Fort Kearney, by order of the President of the United States, dated the ninth of April, eighteen hundred and forty-six, and therefore illegal, viz: First. The west half of northwest quarter of section thirty, township sixty-eight north, range forty-three west, by John Boulware, per cash certificate number twelve hundred and fifty-six, dated January two, eighteen hundred and fifty-four. Second. The northwest quarter of southeast quarter of section thirty, township sixty-eight north, range forty-three west, by William C. Fowlkes, per cash certificate number twenty-six hundred and ninety, dated June one, eighteen hundred and fifty-four. Third. The southeast quarter of northwest quarter and northeast quarter of southwest quarter of section thirty, township sixty-eight, range forty-three west, by William C. Fowlkes, per cash certificate number eighteen hundred and twenty-nine, date April thirteen, eighteen hundred and fifty-four. Fourth. The southeast quarter of south west quarter of section thirty, township sixty-eight, range forty-three west, by Allen A. Brodford, per cash certificate number twenty-six hundred and ninety-one, dated June twenty-one, eighteen hundred and fifty-four. Fifth. Lot number one of section thirty-one, township sixty-eight, range forty-three west, by William 0. Fowlkes, per cash certificate number six hundred and twenty-three, dated July twenty-seven, eighteen hundred and fifty-three. Sixth. Lots number two, three and four, of section thirty-one, township sixty-eight, range forty-three west, by Simeon Hargis, per cash certificate number eighteen hundred and thirty, dated April thirteen, eighteen hundred and fifty-four. Seventh. Lot number one, of section thirty-two, township sixty-eight, range forty-three west, by Simeon Hargis, per cash certificate number eighteen hundred and thirty-one, dated April thirteen, eighteen hundred and fifty-four. Eighth. Lot number one, in section twenty-four, township sixty-eight, range forty-four west, by George W. Boulware, per cash certificate number nine hundred and thirteen, dated September twenty-six, eighteen hundred and fifty-three. Ninth. Lots one and two, of section twenty-five, township sixty-eight, range forty-four west, by George W. Boulware, per cash certificate number nine hundred and twelve, dated September twenty-six, eighteen hundred and fifty-three. Tenth. Lot number one, of section thirty-six, township sixty-eight, range forty-four west, by George W. Boulware, per cash certificate number nine hundred and fourteen, dated September twenty-six, eighteen hundred and fifty-three. Eleventh. The southeast quarter of section twenty-five, township sixty-eight, range forty-four west, by George W. Boulware, per cash certificate number three hundred and four, dated July nine, eighteen hundred and fifty-three. Twelfth. The west half of south-west quarter of section thirty, township sixty-eight, range forty-three west, selected as swamp land. And whereas the Secretary of War, by letter under date of the eleventh of March, eighteen hundred and seventy, advised the Secretary of the Interior ''that the United States military reservation at Fort Kearney, on the Missouri River, is no longer required for military purposes;'' and whereas the register and receiver at Council Bluffs, Iowa, have reported, under date of May twenty-three, eighteen hundred and seventy, to the General Land Office, that, due notice having been given to all persons having any interest in the same to appear before them on the eighteenth day of May, eighteen hundred and seventy, and show cause why the above-named entries should not be confirmed by act of Congress, no adverse claimants appeared before them: Therefore,

title: A Bill To confirm the title to certain lands on the Fort Kearney military reservation in Fremont County, Iowa.

Mr. Logan, on leave, introduced the following bill: A Bill To incorporate the Irish Colonization Association. Whereas it is of the utmost importance to the welfare and prosperity of the country that the surplus and unemployed population of the eastern and seaboard cities of the United States should be encouraged, aided, and assisted in moving to, settling on, and cultivating the unoccupied and undeveloped lands of the States and Territories of the United States, thus making it producing instead of consuming, while adding to the wealth, resources, and revenues of the country, and thereby raising a prosperous, intelligent, and industrious class of citizens; and whereas the labor of the country is not distributed according to its necessities, and multitudes able and willing to work glut the overcrowded labor markets of the large cities, and with difficulty eke out a scanty subsistence for their families, the latter constantly exposed to the snares and temptations of such a condition, while their situation is hourly aggravated by the large influx of emigrants to our shores, who for lack of knowledge or means remain in the large cities of the seaboard to swell the column of destitution and imbitter rather than improve their condition, while at the same time, through the misrepresentations of designing politicians, from being the warm and enthusiastic advocates of the liberty of their fellow men, at heart they here become the advocates and defenders of tyranny; and whereas the United States, through the homestead and pre-emption laws, have placed it in the power of the humblest citizen to become an owner of the soil, thus encouraging the poor man to flee from the contaminations, morally and politically, of the slums of eastern and seaboard city life, and thereby enabling him to raise his family a credit to the country, instead of (as but too often happens) adding their quota to the criminal calendars; and whereas thousands look in vain for a channel of escape from the sad circumstances of their present situation, and would gladly embrace the opportunity that might be afforded them by an organized medium of assistance that would enable them and their families to avail themselves of the benefits and blessings intended to be diffused under the homestead and pre-emption laws: Therefore,

title: A Bill To incorporate the Irish Colonization Association.

Mr. Banks, on leave, introduced the following bill: A Bill For the promotion of commerce and amity between the people of the United States and of Mexico, by encouraging the citizens of the United States to aid Mexico in the development of her resources. Whereas the peaceful and rapid development of Mexico under her own government, and the prosperity and happiness of her people is earnestly desired by the people of the United States, and demanded by the best interest of both countries, and by the progress of free institutions; and whereas we are led to believe that, in a country like Mexico, sparsely settled and without inland navigation, without an adequate supply of currency for its business, immigration, railroads, and a national currency would powerfully and efficaciously favor these desirable ends; and whereas we are led to believe that the government and the thinking people of Mexico earnestly desire the establishment of such a currency and the construction of railroads, and are proposing to offer franchises and privileges to induce American citizens and American capital, to undertake these great and beneficent public works; and whereas it is represented that American capital and skill would respond to these invitations, and promptly commence to do what would conduce so greatly to the prosperity, happiness, and practical fraternity of both peoples, provided solemn assurances of good will and earnest desire therefor came from the government of the United States, as well as from the government of Mexico: Therefore, to testify the earnest desire of the government and people of the United States for the progress of a sister republic, and for the happiness and prosperity of Mexican people, and to encourage our people by their capital and enterprise to aid in promoting the same.

title: A Bill For the promotion of commerce and amity between the people of the United States and of Mexico, by encouraging the citizens of the United States to aid Mexico in the development of her resources.

latestAction.text: Read twice, referred to the Committee on Claims, and ordered to be printed. Mr. Adams, on leave, introduced the following bill: A Bill For the benefit of T. T. Garrard and others. Whereas, on the twenty-first day of October, eighteen hundred and sixty-two an order was issued by Major General Buell, then commanding the fifteenth army corps, department of the Cumberland, for the destruction of the salt works on Goose Creek near Manchester, Kentucky. And whereas the military forces of the United States, in pursuance of said order, did on the twenty-third and twenty-fourth days of October, eighteen hundred and sixty-two, as effectually as possible, destroy said salt works and also upwards of thirty thousand bushels of manufactured salt, then on hand, in order to prevent the rebel forces from taking possession of same and operating said salt works for the supply of the rebel armies with salt. And whereas the owners and occupants of said salt works, are, and ever have been, devotedly and intensely loyal to the government of the United States, and have sustained great loss in consequence of the injuries done to their said salt works and the destruction of their salt and other property, all of which more fully appears from the orders and reports of the officers who ordered and superintended the destruction of said property, and from the report of William B. Thomasson, commissioner appointed by the War Department to investigate and report as to the value of the property destroyed, and as to the loyalty of the claimants, and so forth: Therefore,

title: A Bill For the benefit of T. T. Garrard and others.

Moore, on leave, introduced the following bill: A Bill To authorize the adjustment of pension claims upon a gold basis. Whereas, on the breaking out of the war for the suppression of the late rebellion, this government entered into the most solemn obligations to capitalists, who were induced upon the faith of the government pledged, to loan money for the prosecution of the war to a successful termination, and thereby preserve the, integrity and life of the nation, which obligations the government has, from time to time, expressed its determination to abide by and fulfill to the very letter; and whereas the government did likewise enter into obligations, as solemnly and earnestly expressed, if not in forms of as strong legal force, to induce loyal citizens to enlist and fight its battles, and put in peril their lives, and the dearest interests of their families, and, indeed, their entire substance, while capitalists, and men of means, who with their families, during the terrible strife, remained in safe places, contributed only of their abundance; and whereas it is exceedingly desirable for a nation to abide by its obligations in good faith, abating in nothing effecting either the weak or the strong, the poor or the sick, and more especially those who, in the darkest hour of peril, stood in arms between the nation's life and its enemies; and whereas the salvation of the country was as absolutely dependent upon brave men at the front, as upon capitalists in the rear: Therefore,

title: A Bill To authorize the adjustment of pension claims upon a gold basis.

Reported back without amendment, ordered to be printed with report and recommitted to the Committee on the Public Lands. Mr. Julian, on leave, introduced the following bill: A Bill To confirm to J. M. Hutchings and J. C. Lamon their pre-emption claims in the Yosemite Valley, in the State of California. Whereas the government of the United States did, by act of Congress approved June thirtieth, eighteen hundred and sixty-four, cede to the State of California the ''cleft'' or ''gorge'' known as the ''Yosemite valley,'' in Mariposa county, California; and whereas prior to said cession J. M. Hutching's and J. C. Lamon had in good faith settled in said valley, with the intention of claiming one hundred and sixty acres each of the public domain under the pre-emption laws of the United States, as soon as said lands should be subject to entry, and they being the only settlers therein: and whereas the said Hutchings and Lamon have resided on and been in possession of the lands thus claimed by them, and have made permanent and substantial improvements thereon to the great convenience and comfort of visitors to said valley, without which the same would be a remote and solitary wilderness; and whereas the said Hutchings and Lamon would unquestionably have been entitled to their pre-emption claims in said valley had the land remained public domain, and the State having succeeded to the rights of the federal government, by gift, in the said valley, cannot afford to be less generous; and whereas it would be improper for the State to erect and keep hotels or other stopping-places in said valley, and a ten years' lease, as contemplated in the act of cession, is wholly inadequate to induce private capital to do so; and whereas, in view of the premises, and as an act of simple justice to the said Hutchings and Lamon, the legislature of the State of California did, by an act which became a law February twentieth, eighteen hundred and sixty-eight, grant to the parties aforesaid the same land they would have been entitled to under the general pre-emption laws, to wit: one hundred and sixty acres each; which act was to take effect and be in force from and after its ratification by the Congress of the United States: Therefore,

title: A Bill To confirm to J. M. Hutchings and J. C. Lamon their pre-emption claims in the Yosemite valley, in the State of California.

Whereas John Martin, a citizen of the Territory of New Mexico, in having, at his own great risk and expense, sunk a well, and obtained a copious supply of pure water, on the Jornada del Muerto, a sterile region of the public domain, in the Territory of New Mexico, whereby the said John Martin has demonstrated the practicability of redeeming, and bringing within the pale of civilization and culture, a vast region of sterile country upon which the government of the United States has heretofore made frequent and expensive, but fruitless efforts to obtain water, with a view of rendering said sterile region, fertile, habitable and valuable: Therefore,

title: A Bill Donating ten sections of public land to John Martin, for services in demonstrating the practicability of obtaining water on the Jornada del Muerto, a desert, in New Mexico.

latestAction.text: Read twice, referred to the Committee on Commerce, and ordered to be printed Mr. Paine, on leave, introduced the following bill: A Bill To authorize the Secretary of War to provide for taking meteorological observations at the military stations in the interior of the continent, and for giving notice on the northern lakes and Atlantic seaboard of the approach and force of storms. Whereas the record of marine disasters on the northern lakes for the years eighteen hundred and sixty-eight and eighteen hundred and sixty-nine, shows that during the year eighteen hundred and sixty-eight one thousand one hundred and sixty-four casualties occurred, involving a loss of three hundred and twenty-one lives, and of property of the value of three million one hundred and fourteen thousand dollars, and that during the year eighteen hundred and sixty-nine, one thousand nine hundred and fourteen casualties occurred, involving a loss of two hundred and nine lives, and of property of the value of four million one hundred and sixty thousand dollars; and that in eighteen hundred and sixty-eight one hundred and five vessels, of the value of one million two hundred and seven thousand three hundred dollars were totally lost, and in eighteen hundred and sixty-nine, one hundred and twenty-six vessels of the value of one million four hundred and fourteen thousand two hundred dollars were totally lost; and whereas scientific observations have already shown that the course of storms in the United States is generally from west to east, and made known their rate of progress, and the changes of the barometer which precede and accompany them; and whereas a large proportion of the loss of life and property by marine disasters on the northern lakes might be avoided by timely notice to mariners of approaching storms: Therefore,

title: A Bill To authorize the Secretary of War to provide for taking meteorological observations at the military stations in the interior of the continent, and for giving notice on the northern lakes and Atlantic seaboard of the approach and force of storms.

latestAction.text: Read twice, referred to the Committee on Military Affairs, and ordered to be printed. Mr. J. H. Moore, on leave, introduced the following bill: A Bill To authorize the payment of bounty to certain volunteer officers of the army who served in the late war for the suppression of the rebellion. Whereas many soldiers who enlisted into the service of the United States, as privates, to serve three years or during the war for the suppression of the late rebellion, were mustered out to receive appointment as commissioned officers, thereby forfeiting their claim to bounty, and whereas in many instances such soldiers received pay but a short time as officers, having been discharged on account of wounds received in action, and having actually, in some cases, realized less compensation from the government than they would have received had they continued to serve as privates, or non-commissioned officers; and whereas, many of these brave and gallant defenders of their country are, at this day, in consequence of wounds received in the line of duty, rendered incapable of support and almost wholly dependent upon the small pension they receive from government for their maintenance and the maintenance of their families: Therefore,

title: A Bill To authorize the payment of bounty to certain volunteer officers of the army who served in the late war for the suppression of the rebellion.

Mr. Crebs, on leave, introduced the following bill: A Bill To aid in building a soldiers' monument at the national cemetery near Mound City, Illinois. Whereas the general government of the United States has purchased and now holds title to a plat of ground near Mound City, in the State of Illinois, and has buried there the remains of five thousand one hundred and forty brave men, who fell in upholding the principles of the Constitution which our fathers made and willed to us, then children, as a sacred legacy; and whereas it is due to their memory that their names and honorable deeds should be transmitted to posterity engraved upon enduring marble; and whereas the State of Illinois has, by act of her legislature, approved and in force from March twenty-ninth, eighteen hundred and sixty-nine, made an appropriation of twelve thousand five hundred dollars to aid in the building of a suitable monument on the ground so owned by the government where these brave men sleep, provided the general government should also make an appropriation for that purpose; and whereas by said act of the legislature of the State of Illinois, the governor of said State is authorized to appoint three commissioners whose duty it shall be upon conference and agreement with the proper officers of the United States, to adopt a suitable design and plan for the monument to be erected upon the grounds of the said national cemetery aforesaid: Therefore,

title: A Bill To aid in building a soldiers' monument at the national cemetery near Mound City, Illinois.

latestAction.text: Mr. Sprague asked, and by unanimous consent obtained, leave to bring in the following bill; which was read twice, ordered to lie on the table, and be printed. Referred to the Committee on Appropriations.

title: A Bill To provide for loaning the public money, and for other purposes. The liberties and interests of the American people imperatively demand that scarcity of capital and high rates of interest for money shall cease. Government deposits in the national banks throughout the country are so much capital withdrawn from industrial and productive interests and employed in speculative investments; such employment being a consequence of the short time allowed for deposits, necessarily producing a scarcity of capital and making rates of interest high in industrial and productive operations, which operations cannot be restricted in the use of capital to the time thus limited. Capital seeks speculative investment in consequence of absence of profits in industrial and productive enterprise. The great increase of value in city property, and the increase in the erection of buildings in cities, are no signs of general prosperity, but the reverse, as it indicates the absence of profitable employment for capital in industrial and productive pursuits, and its employment in the purchase and sale of city property, giving such property increased value. It is known that industrial and productive enterprises are carried on (if at all) with little or no profit, and as cities can only maintain their valuation by profitable business with the interior, it is clear that such apparently increased value has no solid foundation on which to rest. By concentrating in the treasury in New York all government income and individual and other deposits, and disbursing the same from day to day by loans and payment of government indebtedness, the equilibrium of the money market (interrupted by the withdrawal of money collected by taxes and retired into the treasury) will be restored, and the introduction of such government income into the money market in New York (where the rates of interest are correspondingly established for the whole country) will cause to flow from the treasury a steady and powerful stream of money, and so prevent a scarcity or too great abundance at any one time, and therefore of the employment of capital in speculation, as it is only on a scarcity, or an abundant money market at irregular times, that speculation thrives. Speculation is known to be greatest during the greatest fluctuations in the price of money. The great object to be obtained by a condition of specie payment is the maintenance of a standard and uniform value in the capital employed by the people in their various operations, and as the accumulation of gold in the treasury acts as a. forced check on the advance of the price of gold in the market, the same is rendered more or less ineffectual and fluctuating by the irregular flowing in and out of the treasury of the money received from the people in taxes. The loans and the deposits aforesaid will strengthen the treasury by drawing from the banks and otherwise the money now used in speculation. No operator or combination of operators engaged in speculation will be sufficiently powerful to check or hinder the more powerful movements of the treasury, and their capital, in the absence of speculative opportunities for investment, will seek the level of the rates of interest established for money by the treasury movements, which must gradually work lower and lower; and the capital taken from speculative investment will seek employment in the interior in the industrial and productive pursuits of the people, such employment (when high rates of interest cease) being more profitable and safer. By loans as aforesaid the government will derive a large income for the use of its unemployed funds, at least sufficient to pay for the management of the same, and nearly sufficient to pay the expenses of collecting the revenues, besides giving steadiness, greater abundance, and lower rates of interest to the money market. latestAction.text: Read twice, recommitted to the Committee on Reconstruction, and ordered to be printed. Mr. B. F. Butler, on leave, introduced the following bill: A Bill To enforce the fourteenth amendment to the Constitution and the laws of the United States, and to restore the State of Georgia to the republican government elected under its new constitution. Whereas the legislature in the State of Georgia elected under its new constitution, preparatory to the restoration of that State to its proper place in the Union, and to the admission of senators and representatives in Congress therefrom, has, in violation of the fourteenth amendment to the Constitution of the United States, refused to purge itself of members who by said amendment were prohibited from being such members, and from acting as such, and has permitted and continues to permit such members to act as such; and whereas a majority of the persons in fact composing said legislature has, in violation of said constitution, and of said constitution of Georgia, and in violation of the fundamental principles upon which Congress consented to the restoration aforesaid, expelled from said legislature a large number of its legally qualified members upon the sole ground that they were persons of African blood, and admitted thereto other persons not receiving a majority of the votes of the people; in their places; and whereas it appears that the local authorities in said State are wholly unable or unwilling to protect the lives, liberties, and property of lawful and unoffending citizens of said State from lawless violence, and refrain purposely, or from want of power, from bringing such offenders to justice, whereby it fully appears that the people of the State of Georgia have not complied with the terms, or conformed to the principles upon which its restoration was provided for, and that the government thereof is not in fact republican or regular: Therefore,

title: A Bill To enforce the fourteenth amendment to the Constitution and the laws of the United States, and to restore the State of Georgia to the republican government elected under its new constitution.

Mr. Robinson, on leave, introduced the following bill: A Bill To remove obstructions from the East river, at Hell Gate, in the harbor of New York. Whereas the appropriations of eighty-five thousand dollars made heretofore, at the last session of Congress, has proved totally inadequate even to commence operations on this great national work; and whereas engineers of respectability estimate that it would take from three to five millions of dollars to make a thorough removal of said obstructions; and whereas the number of vessels passing through and over these obstructions for the four months ending November thirty, eighteen hundred and sixty-eight, was nineteen thousand four hundred and eight, with cargoes estimated at five millions four hundred and sixty-six thousand eight hundred tons, and of the value of seven hundred and thirty-six millions seven hundred and six thousand dollars; and whereas it is estimated that one out of every fifty sailing vessels suffers damages from these obstructions; and whereas many thousand persons pass daily through and over these obstructions, where accidents must prove terribly fatal; and whereas if these obstructions were removed a nearer, deeper, and less exposed entrance through the sound to the harbor of New York than that now existing by Sandy Hook would be secured: Therefore,

title: A Bill To remove obstructions from the East river, at Hell Gate, in the harbor of New York.

latestAction.text: Read twice, ordered to be printed, and referred to the Committee on the Public Lands. Mr. Julian, on leave, introduced the following bill: A Bill To aid in ascertaining the value of certain public lands in Story county, in the State of Nevada. Whereas our public lands contain mines of the precious metals which are unsurpassed in richness, and can with proper development be made speedily to enhance the value of all property, and thereby relieve the burdens of the people; and whereas the silver mines on the Comstock lode, in the State of Nevada, have proved more productive than any others known to modern times, and are believed to be inexhaustible in wealth, but owing to the great expense in working them are liable to be abandoned by private enterprise; and whereas they can only be saved therefrom by the construction of a deep working and draining tunnel, which shall at once secure the production of many millions of treasure, and prove as a great index work the continuance of mineral lodes in depth, and the practical importance of thus working them; and whereas the magnitude of such work is beyond the capacity of private enterprise, and if completed will be of vast benefit to the government and the whole people of the United States; and whereas by an act of the legislature of the State of Nevada, approved April four, eighteen hundred and sixty-five, entitled ''An act granting the right of way, and authorizing Adolph Sutro and his associates to construct a mining and draining tunnel,'' certain exclusive privileges of rights of way for the construction of a tunnel into the Comstock lode, from any point to be selected in the foot-hills of the Carson river valley were granted as by reference to said act will more fully appear; and whereas an act of Congress was approved the twenty-fifth day of July, eighteen hundred and sixty-six, entitled ''An act granting to Adolph Sutro the right of way and granting other privileges to aid in the construction of a draining and exploring tunnel to the Comstock lode in the State of Nevada,'' in and by which the right of way and certain other privileges were granted to the said Adolph Sutro, his heirs and assigns, for the purpose of driving a tunnel from some point to be selected by the grantee at the hills near Carson river, within Lyon county, to and beyond the Comstock lode, as by reference to said act of Congress will more fully appear; and whereas it is the purpose and intention of the said A. Sutro and his associates to acquire a charter of incorporation under the laws of the States of New York, California, and Nevada, or of one or more of said States, and to assign, transfer, and set over to said corporation, all and singular, the rights, privileges, and immunities of them, the said Adolph Sutro and associates, now possessed, under the aforesaid legislation, or which may be conferred by the present act of Congress, as soon as said corporation shall be fully organized: Therefore,

title: A Bill To aid in ascertaining the value of certain public lands in Story county, in the State of Nevada.

Mr. Stevens, from the Committee on Reconstruction, reported the following bill: A Bill To provide for the erection of not more than two additional States out of the territory of the State of Texas, and for other purposes. Whereas the people of the State of Texas desire to erect out of the territory of said State two additional States of convenient size; and whereas the people of said State of Texas, in pursuance of an act of Congress passed March two, eighteen hundred and sixty-seven, entitled ''An act for the more efficient government of the rebel States,'' and of the several acts supplementary thereto, have elected delegates to a convention to form a constitution of government for the said State of Texas; and whereas it is desired that the two additional States to be formed out of the territory of the said State of Texas be respectively bounded and named as follows--that is to say: That all that part of the territory of the said State of Texas situate and embraced within the following lines, viz; Beginning at a point in the middle of the channel between Galveston island and Bolivar Point, thence through Galveston bay to the mouth of the San Jacinto river, up the San Jacinto river to its confluence with the eastern fork of the San Jacinto, thence up said eastern fork with the western boundaries of the counties of Liberty and Polk, thence north to the Trinity river, thence up said Trinity river to the mouth of the Bois de Arc or east fork of the Trinity, thence up the said east fork to the northwest corner of the county of Kaufman, thence north to the southwest corner of the county of Fannin, thence north with the western border of Fannin to Red river, thence down said Red river to the eastern boundary of the State of Texas, thence south with the eastern boundary of the State of the Gulf of Mexico, thence west across the gulf to the point of the beginning, be erected into a new State, to be known by the name of the State of East Texas; that all that part of the territory of said State of Texas situate and embraced within the following described limits, viz: Beginning at a point in Pass Cavallo, midway between the island and peninsula of Matagorda, thence thorough Matagorda bay to the Colorado river, thence up the said Colorado river to where it is intersected by parallel thirty-two north latitude, thence due west to the Rio Grande, thence down said Rio Grande to the Gulf of Mexico, thence through the Gulf of Mexico to the point of beginning, be erected into a new State, to be called and known by the name of South Texas; and that all the residue and remainder of the territory of said State of Texas be known by the name of the State of Texas: Therefore,

title: A Bill To provide for the erection of not more than two additional States out of the territory of the State of Texas, and for other purposes.

Mr. Beaman, from the Committee on Reconstruction, reported the following bill: A Bill To provide for the erection of two additional States out of the territory of the State of Texas, and for other purposes. Whereas the people of the State of Texas desire to erect out of the territory of said State two additional States of convenient size; and whereas the people of said State of Texas, in pursuance of an act of Congress passed March two, eighteen hundred and sixty-seven, entitled, ''An act for the more efficient government of the rebel States,'' and of the several acts supplementary thereto, have elected delegates to a convention to form a constitution of government for the said State of Texas; and whereas it is desired that the two additional States to be formed out of the territory of the said State of Texas be respectively bounded and named as follows--that is to say: That all that part of the territory of the said State of Texas situate and embraced within the following lines, viz: Beginning at a point in the middle of the channel between Galveston island and Bolivar Point, thence through Galveston bay to the mouth of the San Jacinto river, up the San Jacinto river to its confluence with the eastern fork of the San Jacinto, thence up said eastern fork with the western boundaries of the countries of Liberty and Polk, thence north to the Trinity river, thence up said Trinity river to the mouth of the Bois de Arc or east fork of the Trinity, thence up the said fork to the northwest corner of the county of Kaufman, thence north to the southwest corner of the county of Fannin, thence north with the western border of Fannin to Red river, thence down said Red river to the eastern boundary of the State of Texas, thence south with the eastern boundary of the State to the Gulf of Mexico, thence west across the gulf to the point of the beginning, be erected into a new State, to be known by the name of the State of East Texas; that all that part of the territory of said State of Texas situate and embraced within the following described limits, viz; Beginning at a point in Pass Cavallo, midway between the island and peninsula of Matagorda, thence through Matagorda bay to the Colorado river, thence up the said Colorado river to where it is intersected by parallel thirty-two north latitude, thence due west to the Rio Grande, thence down said Rio Grande to the Gulf of Mexico, thence through the Gulf of Mexico to the point of beginning, be erected into a new State, to be called and known by the name of South Texas; and that all the residue and remainder of the territory of said State of Texas be known by the name of the State of Texas: Therefore,

title: A Bill To provide for the erection of two additional States out of the territory of the State of Texas, and for other purposes.

Mr. Shellabarger, on leave, introduced the following bill: A Bill To alter the laws of Ohio as to the manner of electing representatives in Congress. Whereas, by the constitution of the State of Ohio, persons of African descent, but having a preponderance of white blood, and who have the other qualifications of electors in said State, are electors therein and entitled to vote for members of the most numerous branch of the general assembly of such State, and for representatives from such State in Congress; and whereas on the sixteenth day of April, anno Domini eighteen hundred and sixty-eight, the general assembly of said State passed an act entitled ''An act supplementary to the act entitled 'An act to preserve the purity of elections, passed March twenty, eighteen hundred and forty-one, and to protect the judges in discharge of their duties,''' and which was manifestly designed to, and which, if enforced, does in fact render it impracticable for such electors to vote at any election in said State, and which act has been, for that reason, declared by the supreme court of Ohio to be in violation of the constitution of said State and void; and whereas by the Constitution of the United States the Congress may at any time, by law, make or alter the regulations of any State as to the time, place, and manner of holding elections for representatives in Congress; now to the end that all the legal electors of said State may be permitted freely to vote for such representatives without any hindrance from the act aforesaid,

title: A Bill To alter the laws of Ohio as to the manner of electing representatives in Congress.

Ashley, on leave, introduced the following bill: A Bill To aid in the construction of the Sutro tunnel, in the State of Nevada. Whereas our mines of the precious metals are unsurpassed in richness, and can, with proper development, be made speedily to enhance the value of all property, and thereby relieve the burdens of the people and finally extinguish the public indebtedness; and whereas the silver mines on the Comstock lode, in the State of Nevada, have proved more productive than any others known to modern times, and are believed to be inexhaustible in wealth, but owing to the great expense of working them are liable to be abandoned by private enterprise; and whereas they can only be saved therefrom by the construction of a deep working and draining tunnel, which shall at once secure the production of many millions of treasure, and prove as a great index work the continuance of mineral lode in depth, and the practical importance of thus working them; and whereas the magnitude of such work is beyond the capacity of private enterprise, and if completed will be of vast benefit to the government and the whole people of the United States; and whereas by an act of the legislature of the State of Nevada, approved April four, eighteen hundred and sixty-five, entitled ''An act granting the right of way, and authorizing A. Sutro and his associates to construct a mining an draining tunnel,'' certain exclusive privileges of rights of way for the construction of a tunnel into the Comstock lode, from any point to be selected in the foot-hills of the Carson river valley were granted as by reference to said act will more fully appear; and whereas an act of Congress was approved the twenty-fifth day of July, eighteen hundred and sixty-six, entitled ''An act granting to A. Sutro the right of way and granting other privileges to aid in the construction of a draining and exploring tunnel to the Comstock lode in the State of Nevada,'' in and by which the right of way and certain other privileges were granted to the said A. Sutro, his heirs and assigns, for the purpose of driving a tunnel from some point to be selected by the grantee at the hills near Carson river, within Lyon county, to and beyond the Comstock lode, as by reference to said act of Congress will more fully appear; and whereas it is the purpose and intention of the said A. Sutro and his associates to acquire a charter of incorporation under the laws of the States of New York, California, and Nevada, or of one or more of said States, and to assign, transfer, and set over to said corporation, all and singular, the rights, privileges, and immunities of them the said A. Sutro and associates now possessed, under the aforesaid legislation, or which may be conferred by the present act of Congress, as soon as said corporation shall be fully organized: Therefore,

title: A Bill To aid in the construction of the Sutro tunnel, in the State of Nevada.

Mr. Loan, on leave, introduced the following bill: A Bill To provide levees to secure the lowlands of Arkansas and Missouri from inundation, and to encourage the settlement thereof. Whereas the Memphis and Saint Louis Railroad Company, (a corporation created by and existing under the laws of the State of Arkansas,) and the Southeast Missouri Railroad Company, (a corporation created by and existing under the laws of the State of Missouri,) propose to construct a railroad from a point at the commencement of the lowlands to the southwest of Capt Girardeau, in the State of Missouri, along the west bank of the Mississippi river to the mouth of the Saint Francis river, in the State of Arkansas; the road-bed of which shall be so constructed as to serve the purpose of a levee between said points; they further propose to furnish the landless in that region with immediate employment at fair wages in the construction of such levee and road-bed, and to give those thus employed the right to purchase, at fair prices, of the lands of said companies along the route of said levee and railroad, (of which said companies own five hundred thousand acres,) a homestead for each, of as much as forty acres of land: Therefore,

title: A Bill To provide levees to secure the lowlands of Arkansas and Missouri from inundation, and to encourage the settlement thereof.

Mr. Ward, on leave, introduced the following bill: A Bill Fixing the time for the election of Representatives in Congress, to amend the naturalization laws, and to detect fraudulent naturalization papers. Whereas it is expedient for Congress to exercise the power conferred upon it by the fourth section of article one of the Constitution of the United States, of making regulations concerning the time, places, and manner of holding elections for representatives to Congress; and whereas recent developments have shown that gross violations of the naturalization laws have been committed by State courts in the large cities and towns of the Union, and a great number of fraudulent naturalization papers are abroad through the country and have been used by persons not legal voters, and are liable to be still further used by such persons in fraud of the rights of legal voters, and if this evil is permitted to continue in the future it can only end in the subversion of the right of suffrage and the overthrow of the government: Therefore,

title: A Bill Fixing the time for the election of Representatives in Congress, to amend the naturalization laws, and to detect fraudulent naturalization papers.
