Mr. Benton, on leave, introduced the following bill: A Bill To make partial compensation for expenses incurred in the prosecution of the war by providing for the taxation of national bonds. Whereas certain war expenses have been necessarily incurred by the loyal population in the national defence; and whereas, in consequence of the men capable of, and liable to military duty not being in proportion to the population in the several States, there was a similar want of proportion in said expenses; and whereas it is impossible exactly to equalize said expenses upon a just basis; and whereas it is competent for the federal government to equalize them approximately and as far as practicable, and to pay them by an appropriation of the proceeds of a federal tax; and whereas the federal government has exercised, and now possesses, the right and power to tax the bonds, notes, certificates of indebtedness, and other moneyed securities of the United States in the hands of the owners or holders hereof; and whereas the owners and holders of such securities desire the removal of the cause of agitations which impair and threaten the saleable value of such securities, and the increase of such saleable value, by the taxation of such securities at a higher rate than heretofore by the (authority of the) federal government: Therefore

title: A Bill To make partial compensation for expenses incurred in the prosecution of the war by providing for the taxation of national bonds.

Hooper, on leave, introduced the following bill: A Bill For the admission of Deseret into the Union. Whereas the people of the Territory of Utah did by their representatives form for themselves a constitution and State government, republican in form, which was ratified by the people of said Territory at an election held for that purpose in pursuance of law, on the fourth day of February, anno Domini eighteen hundred and sixty-seven; and whereas the legislative assembly of the proposed State of Deseret did petition as follows: To the honorable the Senate and House of Representatives of the United States of America in Congress assembled: Gentlemen: We, your memorialists, the members of the general assembly of the State of Deseret, respectfully state that our peculiarly isolated position, the well-proven inadequacy of a territorial organization to meet the wants of a numerous and rapidly increasing population, a disposition to lessen governmental expenditures, and an earnest desire to enjoy those inherent, inalienable, and constitutional rights guaranteed to every American citizen, have induced the citizens of Utah to unanimously and constitutionally organize a State government, preparatory to their admission into the Union as the State of Deseret: Wherefore your memorialists most respectfully solicit your honorable body to favorably consider this, our petition, and, at as early a day as other important duties will permit, take action admitting the State of Deseret into the Union, on an equal footing with the original States. And, as in duty bound, your memorialists will ever pray.

title: A Bill For the admission of Deseret into the Union.

Mr. Hogan, from the Committee of Ways and Means, reported the following bill: A Bill To compensate the North Missouri Railroad Company, of Missouri, for losses sustained during the rebellion in performing government service, and to allow a credit on duties to be paid upon imported railroad iron. Whereas the North Missouri railroad, in the State of Missouri, in the years eighteen hundred and sixty-two, eighteen hundred and sixty-three, and eighteen hundred and sixty-four, was at various times attacked and raided upon by rebel forces, acting at times under orders from officers in the regular service of the confederate authorities, and at times as lawless guerillas, and was greatly damaged in the burning of cars, depots, repair shops, and bridges, and in the tearing up and destruction of its track, whereby the railroad company sustained a loss in material and business exceeding one million of dollars; and whereas said railroad company, in its officers and employees, was at all times loyal to the government of the United States, and did all in its power to aid the authorities of the United States in suppressing the rebellion, by transporting troops, arms, and ammunition, and thereby did efficient service for the United States, and in consequence incurred the hostility of rebels and their sympathizers to such an extent as to induce the attacks and destruction of property aforesaid; and whereas said railroad was not adequately protected by the forces of the United States while so engaged in government service, nor were the damages aforesaid, in whole or in part, repaired or repaid by the United States, nor has said railroad company received from the United States any compensation or equivalent therefor; and whereas said railroad company is now engaged in changing and rebuilding portions of its road so damaged as aforesaid and in extending its road northward so as to connect it with railroads in the State of Iowa, and also, by branches running east and west, to connect it with railroads in Kansas and Illinois, and for these purposes is engaged in importing railroad iron: Therefore--

title: A Bill To compensate the North Missouri Railroad Company, of Missouri, for losses sustained during the rebellion in performing government service, and to allow a credit on duties to be paid upon imported railroad iron.

Whereas, in the year of our Lord one thousand eight hundred and sixty-one, the citizens of the States of South Carolina, North Carolina, Georgia, Florida, Alabama, Mississippi, Louisiana, Texas, Arkansas, and Virginia, being a portion of the United States of America, did violently set aside and destroy the organized constitutional governments of said States, and did engage in armed hostility and warfare, to maintain a separate and independent government from that of the United States; and whereas, after the lapse of more than four years, the United States, by force of arms, having succeeded in destroying said separate government, and quelling rebellion, and disarming such insurgent citizens, did find in said States no government organized, or officers qualified, according to the requirements of the Constitution of the United States; and whereas, the President of the United States, by virtue of his powder as commander-in-chief of the army and navy, under the operation of martial law, for the purpose of preserving peace and order, and of relieving his subordinate military officers from executing, details of the civil regulations in the several States, did, under forms and rules by him prescribed, authorize certain citizens of the said States to assume the execution of said purpose of preserving peace and order under the protection and sanction of the military authority; and whereas it is the duty of the Congress of the United States of America, to preserve the said States and the citizens thereof as a part of the United States, and by law to cause to be organized therein governments republican in form, based upon the civil and law-making power of the nation: Therefore--

title: A Bill To re-establish civil governments in the States lately in rebellion, and enable them to resume their former relations with the States of the American Union.

latestAction.text: Read twice, referred to the Committee on Reconstruction, and ordered to be printed. Mr. H. D. Washburn, on leave, introduced the following bill: A Bill To re-establish civil government in the States of Virginia, North Carolina, South Carolina, Georgia, Florida, Alabama, Mississippi, Arkansas, Louisiana and Texas, and to restore said States to the possession and exercise of political and representative power in the federal Union. Whereas the rebellion lately waged by the people of the States of Virginia, North Carolina, South Carolina, Georgia, Florida, Alabama, Mississippi, Arkansas, Louisiana and Texas, against the government of the United States, deprived the people of the above-named States of all rightful civil government; and whereas the said rebellion did not deprive the government of the United States of its constitutional jurisdiction over the territory of said States, and over the people thereof; and whereas the fourth section of the fourth article of the Constitution of the United States declares that the United States shall guarantee to every State in the Union a republican form of government; and whereas the restoration of the above-named States to the possession and exercise of political and representative power as members of the federal Union, under governments republican in form, is a duty which appertains, under the Constitution, to the Congress of the United States; and whereas Congress is solemnly bound to assume the responsibility of this work of reconstruction, and to employ, if need be, all its powers for its successful consummation, and to take care that in the performance of this duty loyalty is advanced and protected everywhere throughout the States lately in rebellion, and that the new governments to be established are founded upon the fundamental truths that all men are equal in rights, and that all just governments stand only on the consent of the governed; and because the measures for reconstruction which originated in the executive power of the government have failed to accomplish the necessary ends, but on the contrary have resulted in the establishment of governments in the above-named States, derived from that hostile population lately engaged in armed rebellion, in the exclusion, as a general rule, of loyal men from office, and in the denial of civil and political rights to large masses of loyal citizens, so that treason is made respectable and loyalty a disgrace; and because almost all of the governments of the above-named States, so established through executive agency, have rejected, and the remainder failed to ratify, wholesome and necessary amendments of the national Constitution, proposed by Congress in a spirit of kindness, with a view to reconstruction, and the more effectually to secure union, establish justice, insure domestic tranquility, promote the general welfare, and extend the blessings of liberty, by which course the said governments have manifested a spirit of opposition to the declared objects of the Constitution: Therefore,

title: A Bill To re-establish civil government in the States of Virginia, North Carolina, South Carolina, Georgia, Florida, Alabama, Mississippi, Arkansas, Louisiana and Texas, and to restore said States to the possession and exercise of political and representative power in the federal Union.

Mr. Stevens, on leave, introduced the following bill: A Bill To re-establish civil government in North Carolina, and enable it to resume its former relations as one of the constituent States of the American Union. Whereas, on the twentieth day of May, anno Domini eighteen hundred and sixty-one, the citizens of North Carolina, one of the United States of America, did rebel against the government of the United States, and on the said twentieth day of May and thereafter, did violently set aside and destroy the organized constitutional government of said State, and did engage with others in armed hostility and warfare to maintain their said action; and whereas, after the lapse of more than four years, the United States, by force of arms, having succeeded in quelling said rebellion and disarming such insurgent citizens, did find in said district, formerly comprising the State of North Carolina, no government organized, or officers qualified, according to the requirements of the Constitution of the United States; and whereas the President of the United States, by virtue of his power as commander-in-chief of the army and navy, under the operation of martial law, for the purpose of preserving peace and order, and of relieving his subordinate military officers from executing details of the civil regulations in the several and widely separated localities in the district, did, under forms and rules by him prescribed, authorize certain citizens of the district to assume the execution of said purpose of preserving peace and order under the protection and sanction of the military authority; and whereas it is the duty of the Congress of the United States of America, to preserve the said district and the loyal citizens thereof as one of the United States, and by law to cause to be organized therein a government republican in form, based upon the civil and law making power of the nation: Therefore--

title: A Bill To re-establish civil government in North Carolina, and enable it to resume its former relations as one of the constituent States of the American Union.

latestAction.text: Read twice, referred to the Committee on Public Lands, and ordered to be printed. Mr. McRuer, on leave, introduced the following bill: A Bill To confirm title to certain lands in California and provide for survey of same. Whereas in California many grantees of land from the Mexican government had, prior to anno Domini eighteen hundred and fifty-two, sold and conveyed the greater part, if not all, of the land granted to them to different persons; and whereas in such cases many persons who had purchased specific portions of such grants were advised by federal officers and attorneys at law that it was not necessary to present each his separate claim for confirmation to the ''Board of Commissioners to ascertain and settle private land claims in California,'' and, in consequence of such advice, many did not present their claims for land, who held under valid deeds from the original grantees of the Mexican government; and whereas in such cases one or more persons holding deeds from the original grantee did present to the said board their specific claims for confirmation, and did obtain confirmation thereof, thereby calling in question the validity of the entire grant: Now therefore--

title: A Bill To confirm title to certain lands in California and provide for survey of same.
